Post-endodontic pain

PBM may modestly reduce pain one day after some root-canal procedures, but randomized trials also report null results in emergency and surgical settings.

Summary of the Evidence

PBM may modestly reduce short-term pain after some root-canal procedures. A 2026 review found a small average one-day benefit versus placebo, while individual trials report both favorable and null results across different diagnoses and comparators.

Human and clinical evidence

The exact database category contains 33 titles: 23 randomized clinical reports, one rat study, eight reviews or syntheses, and one protocol. Otaify et al. was tagged as a comparison study in the database, but the primary report describes computer-generated random assignment; it is counted as randomized. Reviews overlap primary trials. A separate pulpotomy category is not included in this total.

A 2026 systematic review assessed nine studies, five at low risk of bias. Eight studies favored laser therapy; five were pooled against placebo. The one-day visual analogue scale mean difference was −0.56 (95% CI −0.74 to −0.38; I² = 31%). This estimate suggests a modest short-term effect and does not establish benefit for every endodontic diagnosis (Bonacina et al. 2026).

Recent randomized trials conflict. In 80 single-visit root-canal patients, Reddy et al. reported 24-hour VAS scores of 2.1 ± 1.2 with PBM and 4.8 ± 1.5 with placebo, together with lower analgesic use (Reddy et al. 2026). A 70-person emergency-pulpectomy trial in symptomatic irreversible pulpitis found no overall postoperative-pain reduction (Freitas-Júnior et al. 2026). Otaify et al. randomized 48 patients with symptomatic apical periodontitis to laser therapy or calcium hydroxide; 46 were analyzed, and no significant between-group differences were found for pain or inflammatory markers (Otaify et al. 2026).

A 90-person trial in asymptomatic first molars found no significant pain or analgesic-use difference between PBM, saline, and cryotherapy; low baseline pain may have limited the ability to detect a difference (Kalena et al. 2026). In a related trial after apical surgery, 36 participants received PBM plus placebo ibuprofen or simulated PBM plus ibuprofen. Pain and analgesic use did not differ significantly; this study is supplemental and outside the exact database count (Cirisola et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

One rat publication is indexed in the exact category. It is indirect evidence and cannot establish postoperative pain relief in people.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols differ in diagnosis, treatment site, light delivery, comparator, and timing. Recent examples include 808-nm diode-laser treatment after single-visit root-canal care or emergency pulpectomy, a 940-nm protocol applied at four mucosal sites, and intracanal laser therapy compared with calcium hydroxide. These approaches are not interchangeable. Trials compare PBM with placebo, active treatment, or usual care and use different pain-assessment intervals.

Interpretation

The pooled placebo-controlled estimate supports a possible modest reduction in pain at one day, while several recent randomized trials found no overall advantage in distinct clinical settings. Certainty is low for short-term pain after root-canal treatment and very low for emergency pulpectomy or post-apical-surgery pain. Better trials should stratify by diagnosis, use credible sham controls where possible, standardize pain and analgesic-use measures, and distinguish statistical from clinically important effects.

Otaify et al. 2026 was classified as randomized after checking its allocation method. Review records overlap primary trials.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Post-root-canal pain — pooled one-day VAS mean difference −0.56 (95% CI −0.74 to −0.38; five studies; I² = 31%), favoring laser therapy (Bonacina et al. 2026).

Single-visit root-canal trial — 24-hour VAS 2.1 ± 1.2 with PBM versus 4.8 ± 1.5 with placebo; a separate emergency-pulpectomy trial found no overall pain reduction (Reddy et al. 2026; Freitas-Júnior et al. 2026).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term pain reduction after root-canal treatment versus placebo. Very low for emergency pulpectomy and post-apical-surgery pain.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The 2026 pooled estimate is based on five studies and indicates a modest one-day difference, while recent trials in emergency pulpectomy, symptomatic apical periodontitis, and apical surgery did not show an overall pain advantage. Diagnoses, comparators, treatment sites, pain intervals, and co-interventions differ, and clinical importance is not established. These limits lower confidence in a general effect across endodontic procedures.
